chief_complaint: acute retrosternal chest pain radiating to left arm and sweating for 1 hour
hpi_details: A 26-year-old female presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset retrosternal chest pain radiating to her left arm, accompanied by sweating, for the past 1 hour. She has no traditional cardiovascular risk factors.
ideas: She thinks she is suffering from a massive panic attack triggered by extreme deadlines at work.
concerns: She is terrified that she might collapse and die alone in her apartment before anyone finds her.
expectations: She hopes to get an ECG and fast-acting medicine to make the chest pain stop immediately.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Acute Coronary Syndrome evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Coronary Syndrome is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes obtaining a STAT 12-lead ECG and cardiac enzymes without delay, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: acute retrosternal chest pain radiating to left arm and sweating for 1 hour

Key HPI features: A 26-year-old female presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset retrosternal chest pain radiating to her left arm, accompanied by sweating, for the past 1 hour. She has no traditional cardiovascular risk factors.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: assess for tachycardia, hypotension, or hypoxia. Cardiac auscultation for murmurs or gallops; check for signs of heart failure. STAT 12-lead ECG (looking for ST elevation/depression or new LBBB) and serial high-sensitivity troponin.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Coronary Syndrome.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Aortic dissection without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Ongoing pain, low blood pressure, or new breathlessness.
management_principles: Obtain STAT 12-lead ECG and cardiac enzymes without delay

Give aspirin if not contraindicated; activate the emergency ACS pathway and individualize antiplatelet/reperfusion therapy after ECG, bleeding-risk, and coronary-anatomy assessment (consider SCAD in a young woman without traditional risk factors)
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of acute retrosternal chest pain radiating to left arm and sweating for 1 hour. HPI: myocardial ischemia, plaque rupture.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: assess for tachycardia, hypotension, or hypoxia. Cardiac auscultation for murmurs or gallops; check for signs of heart failure. STAT 12-lead ECG (looking for ST elevation/depression or new LBBB) and serial high-sensitivity troponin.
reference_soap.assessment: Acute Coronary Syndrome in a young woman without traditional cardiovascular risk factors; spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) should be actively considered alongside atherosclerotic ACS given her age and sex. DDx: aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism, oesophageal spasm.
reference_soap.plan: Obtain STAT 12-lead ECG and cardiac enzymes without delay. Give aspirin if not contraindicated; activate the emergency ACS pathway and individualize antiplatelet/reperfusion therapy after ECG, bleeding-risk, and coronary-anatomy assessment (coronary angiography can identify SCAD, which is managed conservatively rather than with stenting in most cases). Consult specialist if symptoms worsen. Counsel patient.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Acute Coronary Syndrome
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Acute Coronary Syndrome

Implement evidence-based management plan: Obtain STAT 12-lead ECG, cardiac enzymes. Give aspirin if not contraindicated; activate the emergency ACS pathway and individualize antiplatelet/reperfusion therapy after ECG, bleeding-risk, and coronary-anatomy assessment

teaching.one_liner: Retrosternal pain from acute coronary obstruction. Time is muscle: the history exists to get to ECG and troponin fast.
differentials: Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) — the leading cause of ACS in young women without traditional risk factors
red_flags: Ongoing pain, low blood pressure, or new breathlessness

must_ask.objective: Site and radiation of the pain
must_ask.say: Where exactly is the pain, and does it move anywhere else?
When did it start, and how long does it last each time?
How would you describe it — sharp, crushing, burning, tight?
Along with the pain, did you feel sweaty, sick, or short of breath?
Do you have high blood pressure, diabetes, or high cholesterol, and do you smoke?
Have you had a heart attack, stent, or bypass before?

history.answer: About an hour ago, I got this sudden, crushing tightness in the middle of my chest and started breaking out in a heavy cold sweat.
It started very suddenly about an hour ago while I was just sitting at my desk working on my computer.
It is right in the center of my chest, deep behind my breastbone, and it covers a wide area that I cannot pinpoint with one finger.
It feels like a heavy, squeezing pressure, as if a heavy weight is pressing down on my chest.
Yes, the ache and tightness shoot down into my left arm toward my wrist.
It has been continuous and unrelenting since it began an hour ago.
I would rate it an 8 out of 10, and it has stayed steadily severe the whole time.
I was completely resting when it hit me, and staying still hasn't helped ease it at all.
Taking deep breaths, coughing, or leaning forward doesn't change it, and pressing on my chest doesn't make it hurt more.
No, I haven't eaten recently, and there is no burning sensation, sour taste, or trouble swallowing.
I am drenched in a cold sweat and feel mildly sick to my stomach, but I haven't vomited or felt like passing out.
No fever, no chills, and no cough or sputum.
No, I haven't had any recent cold, sore throat, or flu-like symptoms.
Neither leg is swollen or painful, and I haven't had any recent surgeries, long trips, or periods of immobility.
No, there is no rash, redness, or blisters on my chest or anywhere on my body.
I feel terrified and anxious that something terrible is happening to my heart, but I don't have tingling in my hands.
I have never had high blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol, or any heart trouble, and I have never smoked.
No, I have never experienced chest pain like this before, and I've never had any heart tests or procedures done.
No, I did not hurt my chest, and I haven't done any heavy lifting or intense exercise recently.
I thought maybe I was having a massive panic attack because work has been so overwhelming lately.
I'm terrified that I might pass out and die alone in my apartment before anyone finds me.
I just want an ECG to check my heart and some strong medication to make this pain stop right away.
I have always been healthy and have never been diagnosed with any medical conditions.
I have never had surgery and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter pills, or supplements.
I have no known allergies to any medications or foods.
I have never smoked cigarettes, e-cigarettes, or used any tobacco products.
I only drink a glass of wine on social occasions once or twice a month, and I do not use illicit drugs.
I work as a graphic designer in an office, and I live in an apartment with my partner.
There is no family history of heart disease, heart attacks at a young age, or sudden unexplained death.
My last period started two weeks ago, and my menstrual cycles are always regular every 28 days.
We use barrier protection, and a routine home pregnancy test last week was negative, so I am definitely not pregnant.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 118/76 mmHg in the right arm and 116/74 mmHg in the left arm, pulse is 96 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation is 98% on room air, and temperature is 36.7 °C.
Young female patient appearing pale, visibly diaphoretic, and in acute distress while clutching her central chest.
Jugular venous pressure is normal with no visible jugular venous distension.
No chest wall abrasions, bruising, or skin lesions; no reproducible tenderness on palpation over the sternum, ribs, or costochondral junctions.
Normal resonance to percussion bilaterally over all lung fields.
Breath sounds are clear bilaterally with no rales, wheezes, or pleural friction rubs.
Regular rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, gallops, or pericardial friction rubs appreciated.
Abdomen is soft, flat, and non-tender throughout with no epigastric tenderness, guarding, or organomegaly.
No edema noted in either lower extremity.
Calves are supple, symmetric, and non-tender with no warmth or erythema bilaterally.
Radial, posterior tibial, and dorsalis pedis pulses are intact, symmetric, and strong bilaterally.
